Not so fast.

First off, all other things being equal (which they are not) we would
expect any given player in a 5-player game to win 20% of the time --
NOT COUNTING TIES! So to simplify our analysis, the first thing to do
is eliminate the ties from consideration, which gives us:

1st seed: 16/53 = 30%
2nd seed: 10/53 = 19%
3rd seed: 8/53 = 15%
4th seed: 8/53 = 15%
5th seed: 11/53 = 21%

Next thing we must take into consideration is that all things are not
equal. The best players with the best decks will tend to win more
often, as well as end up with the top seed more often. We would
expect that, based on skill alone, the top seed would win more than
20% of non-tied final games..

How often the top seed SHOULD win non-tied games, based on the skill
factor alone, is anyone's guess, but it could conceivably be as low as
(say) 25%, or as high as (say) 35% or more.

So we still don't really know if the seating ceremony is increasing a
top seed's chances of victory (due to the seating advantage) or
reducing it (because the ceremony paints a big fat target on his
forehead).

It won't. Not for you, at any rate. But it is also true that there are
some people who do not scout, and will not scout and/or will get
little or no benefit from trying to scouting even if the rule is kept
as is. (Somewhere in between these extremes, there might be folks on
the edge, who might scout less if there were less incentive).

For instance (to take an extreme example), a disabled guy in a
wheelchair, with moderately poor distance vision, poor memory for
faces, and lacking a network of informants, may be effectively unable
to scout, but still be a very good player of the game as it is
normally played.

My point is not that V:tES tournaments should make special allowances
for the handicapped -- but merely that tournament rules should be
geared towards rewarding those who are good at the game as it is
ordinarily played.

> Everyone should scout all the time in all tournaments.

Be careful what you wish for. "Everyone" does not scout, as it is;
most that do do not scout "all the time"; and I do not think Judges
would like it if they did.

> I think trying to
> stop, disincentivize, dissuade, or discourage scouting is just silly.
> Random final or no.

All we are "trying" to do is randomize seating in the finals. And
there is nothing silly about that.

It *might* be silly if we tried to do more than that, for all the
reasons you state, but that's a whole other question.

I could retort "I think trying to promote, incentivise, and encourage
scouting is just silly, Random final or no, because most of the people
who do it are going to do it anyway, and because some people will not
bother no matter what you do."

So why should we keep the current rule? Scouting skills have little
or nothing to do with the game as ordinarily played.

Let me first point out that you are loading the question.

The question is a choice between two seating methods. I could just as
easily ask you, "What problem are you attempting to solve by
eliminating random seating?" Random seating is the norm in V:tES, or
at least, it is usual for seating to be effectively random as to decks
(if not necessarily the players) because seating is almost never
chosen with knowledge of what an opponent is playing. Finals seating
is the exception to the rule. You are able to take the offensive only
because non-random seating has somehow become a 15-year old tradition.

So the question, really is, what seating method do you prefer and
why.

Let's start with a totally subjective and selfish consideration. I
hate scouting. And I am terrible at it. I am one of those people who
(for the most part) does not scout, and when I do I get almost nothing
out of it. Unless I actually sit down and play against a person, I
can rarely remember who is playing what. Thus any rule that helps
scouters is not helping me -- it is only helping my opponents.

Lets move to a second consideration -- also somewhat subjective, but
more theoretical. I am a fan of V:tES, and by V:tES, I mean the
Standard Game. For me, the Standard Game is an end in itself, and any
changes thereto, for tournament purposes, require justification. I
see the purpose of the tournament is to measure skill at standard
V:tES.

Most changes to Standard Rules, for tournament purposes, were caused
by a regrettable necessity -- the time limit. V:tES, in its standard
form, is a kill or be killed, eat or be eaten game. Very rarely will
a completed standard game (especially a 5-player game) end in a tie,
and only the most unlikely situations end with a table being split
1,1,1,1,1. But with a time limit, this can easily be achieved -- all
that need happen is for two hours to pass with no-one being ousted --
or that would be the score if tournaments were scored consistently
with the pattern of the standard rules (with every player who is not
ousted keeping the 1 vp he brought to the table).

Since ties were not in keeping with the eat-or-be-eaten "spirit of the
game", time limits and ties had to be dis-incentivized in time-limited
games. Surviving to time out was only given 0.5 vp as a "risk
incentive". Though this distorted the standard rules, its aim was to
preserve the "spirit" (rather than the letter) of the Standard Rules.
(This change ultimately led to other changes, such as the discounting
of the withdrawal bonus).

I recognize that others (probably you among them, judging by your
earlier comments) do not have this attitude. For some, the tournament
rules have become an end in themselves. For such, it is irrelevant to
you to what extent they accurately reflect the standard rules (spirit
or letter), and to what extent they distort them. I cannot say others
are wrong for this, any more than I can say you would be wrong for
preferring Monopoly. I can only say that I do have a loyalty to
Standard V:tES.

But to those with whom I do have some common ground, in believing the
tournament rules should reflect at least the spirit of the Standard
Game, I have this argument. Scouting is not a skill which is relevant
in the Standard Game. Similarly, the ability to choose your predator
and prey, using knowledge of what they are playing, in the hope of
gaining an advantage, is likewise not a skill that is relevant to the
Standard Game. If the goal of a tournament is to find the best V:tES
player, then rewarding the skill of scouting and the skill of predator-
picking makes as much sense as rewarding beauty, weight lifting
ability, or knowledge of legal theory.

enough for now ...

I share that ground.

A justification for using the current seating method is that the
seating matters. In the preliminary rounds, as in the Standard Game,
there is no basis on which to award seating choice priority, so the
seating choice (with the corresponding advantages and disadvantages it
imparts to each player) is done randomly.

Similarly, choosing who sits at each table is done randomly (again
having no merit basis for distinguishing the players).

For the final however, there is a measure of relative performance for
comparing each player to each other player.

This measure is used to determine who merits a seat at the final table
(rather than leaving that random)
And this measure is used to determine who merits seat choice priority
(rather than leaving that random)

This is done in other competitions, as well, as mentioned in earlier
threads (cf. short track, ski cross, etc.)

Another justification is more akin to bending to the needs of the
tournament (cf. time limits as you mention). In a single game
(Standard Game), players have no reason no to play to win that single
game. In a series-of-games setting (as in the preliminary rounds),
situations may arise due to the tournament's addition of "determining
who goes to the final" that may result in a player having a choice
between improving xeir tournament performance and improving their
single game performance.

We have the sportmanship rule, the PTW portion of which dictates that
the player in such a situation must sacrifice the tournament
performance for the game performance, which is not a good position for
the player to be in and could promote/reward cheating.

As such, reducing the occurrence of such situations is warranted, so
that players are put into such situations less often, if ever.
Increasing the advantage of finishing 1st over finishing 2nd going
into the finals arguably does some of that.

I imagine that the idea, in the sports competitions you mention, is
usually not to INTRODUCE imbalance and unfairness to the final
competition. Rather the idea is that some unfairness is already
inherent in the competition, and, if such unfairness MUST be assigned
to someone, it might as well be assigned on the basis of previous
merit.

If you assign the best start position to just anyone, folks might say
“the only reason he won was because he had the best start position.”
But if you assign the best start position to the top seed, folks are
more likely to say, “Oh well, he was the most likely to win anyway,
since he did best in preliminary rounds, so the ultimate outcome would
probably have been the same.” People are more likely to feel that,
despite unavoidable flaws, the competition has probably served its
purpose – finding the best player.

It is far less likely that such competitions will deliberately
introduce unfairness not already inherent. For instance, I have never
heard that, in the 100 meter dash, the lower-seeded players are forced
to carry five-pound weights. Such measures would only reduce our
confidence that the best player really has won.

Some such “inherent” unfairness can be found in V:tES, in terms of
order of play. For instance, it is universally agreed that going
fifth is a disadvantage. I would have less objection to assigning
such “inherent” unfairness of the basis of previous merit. For
instance, one might have random seating, but still have a rule that
the fifth seed’s prey (whoever that is) goes first, or it could be the
rule that (after relative seating is chosen, but before decks are cut)
the top seed decides who goes first.

Once you separate the “who goes first” question, I see no basis for
the idea that there is ANY inherent unfairness in the random assigning
of predator-prey relationships. If, in Short Track, you randomly
assign starting positions, someone always gets lucky and someone
always gets the short end of the stick. But no claim can be made
that this is necessarily true of random predator-prey assignments in
V:tES. Why cannot such a result be “fair”? It is possible that,
after such random assignment, some of the players (perhaps all of
them) can imagine that a different arrangement could have been more
advantageous to them. But it does not necessarily follow from this
that anyone has been given an “unfair” advantage, or an “unfair”
disadvantage. In fact, it is hard to imagine by what standard such
“unfairness” should be measured.

However, player choice may create unfairness that might not otherwise
existed. Players will not choose fairness because they are not
interested in fairness. They want the result that will ensure their
victory. Thus top-seed seating choice may be more analogous to
forcing lower-seeded sprinters to wear 5 lb weights than it is to
assigning starting positions in Short Track.

For instance, a top seed with a dominate stealth bleed deck, with lost
of wakes and deflections, can place himself between his non-bleed-
bouncing prey and a predator who is also a dominate stealth bleeder
with some wakes and deflections. In this way, he ensures that his
prey will become the bleed-sink for half the table, overwhelming his
defenses.

(Indeed, if he knows or suspects he will be top seed, he can even
throw a bunch of extra deflections in his deck for precisely this
purpose. This is totally cheating, of course, but who’s to know? I
was only ever in one tournament where I was asked to provide a deck-
list in advance).

> Another justification is more akin to bending to the needs of the
> tournament (cf. time limits as you mention).

[snip ]

> As such, reducing the occurrence of such situations is warranted, so
> that players are put into such situations less often, if ever.
> Increasing the advantage of finishing 1st over finishing 2nd going
> into the finals arguably does some of that.

I have more sympathy for this argument (the PTW-incentive argument)
than for the merit argument. I am unsure that anything more than the
tie-breaker advantage is necessary, or that anything beyond that
would be helpful in preventing unsportsmanlike behavior, but if it is,
there may be other ways of creating such incentive.

But the current seating rule has potential to cause trouble too. It
is never good, IMHO, for a player to be able to predict, in advance of
seating, who and what his predator and prey and cross-table buddy will
be. Such advance knowledge gives him the opportunity to make pre-
seating deals (as in the story Jay Kristoff reported), and may even
create too much temptation and incentive to illegally tweak his deck.

argument for randomizing finals seating is false.

Well, okay you have me there. I don't really get how scouting for final

In other words, I don't really see a problem being solved. I don't see
the need for scouting to be any less urgent or for it to be any less of a
handicap for one to under-scout.

In practice almost every tournament in which I play has what I'd
characterize as "light scouting." Most of the players know one another at
least a little bit. The tournaments tend to be small enough that it's
fairly likely to have already played against another finalist. I don't
see anyone sneaking around taking meticulous notes or anything. We don't
take it that seriously. But people will watch games after having
completed theirs. I think we generally do it because we like vtes, not to
gain an advantage.

Here's why I like seating based on rank:

Top seed is the guy to beat. He or she wins on a tie. If you are not top
seed and are not working out how to kill the top seed, then you don't have
your head in the game. 4th and 5th seeds have no choice and will lose
ties (except 4th to 5th, of course, but that hardly ever happens). They
have nothing to lose. The lack of seating choice fits with the desperate
nature of their position. The choice that the higher seeds gets fits with
the position and the winning on ties. All five finalists have roles to
play. While "oust prey" and "don't die" are the obvious goals, "don't let
that lucky bastard win on a tie" is right up there with the rest. Makes
the game more interesting for me.

But I wouldn't consider that reason enough to change to seating based on
rank if we weren't doing that already. Just as I don't consider making
one tiny facet of the world of scouting irrelevant reason enough to change
to random final seating.

Current seating system (vs. random seating)

DISADVANTAGES

Rewards those with superior scouting skills, thereby incorporating a
factor not relevant in the standard game, thereby increasing the
chance that the best player, by standard game standards, will not win.

Seat-picking (based on performance against OTHER players) directly
incorporates a factor not relevant in the standard game, thereby
increasing the chance that the best player, by standard game
standards, will not win.

Discourages PTW: Seating ceremony paints a big fat bullseye-target on
the top seed, thereby providing a DISINCENTIVE to play his best in the
last round of the tournament if he already has 2 GWs.

ADVANTAGES

Encourages PTW: Top-seed seating choice provides an INCENTIVE to play
one's best in the last round of the tournament, even if one already
has 2 GWs.

Requires no dice, cards, or other random generating method. Players
completely handle process, with no judicial input. Cheating or hanky-
panky not an issue or reasonable possibility.

STRAW MEN

It does not cause / encourage scouting - folks would scout anyway.

I’m not sure what we are disagreeing about here. I am perfectly
willing to concede that the top seed is MORE likely to be the best
player than any other finalist.

He has an opportunity to prove this by winning the final game. Even
if he were given no top-seed advantages, I imagine he would win the
(non-tied) final game more than 20% of the time, simply by virtue of
the fact that he has a somewhat more than even chance of being the
better player.

What I don’t understand or agree with is the idea that we should beg
the question by HELPING him win. I don’t agree with allowing the
prediction that he is more likely to win the final game to become a
self-fulfilling prophesy.

> By the same argument, it could be that five players faced 16 total
> cream puffs and sailed to easy 3GW sweeps while the best player faced
> actual competition and would up with 3GW but only 9VPs. So by having a
> cut-off for the finals, you're increasing the chance that the best
> player will not win (by not allowing the best player to play).

I don’t see how it is the “same argument”.

Being in the top five, versus not being in the top five, is roughly
analogous to the idea of being within a “margin of error” as opposed
to being outside that “margin of error”. Margins of error are rarely
absolute and usually somewhat arbitrary, and there is usually a
theoretical possibility that the truth may lie outside it. This
margin is particularly arbitrary, and is dictated by the need for five
players.

Still, there is an excellent chance that the “best player” will indeed
be among those top five (and this chance is far greater than the
chance that the best player is the top seed). If the best player IS
among the top five, then the preliminary rounds have served their
purpose. Now we get a chance to find out which of the top five IS the
best player, and the best way to do that is to give them all an even
playing field. They are being now measured against eachother, perhaps
for the first time.

But one might argue that the final game by itself, fairly played, is
not by itself the BEST indication of who the best player is. Perhaps
we should give a bit more weight to the results of preliminary
rounds. Maybe. But that in itself does not require us tweak the
results of the final game, to unfairly help one player win it. All we
need do is give more weight to the results of preliminary rounds in
computing the “tournament winner” (as distinct from the winner of the
final game).

We have managed to gather together 5 of the most talented and most
evenly matched players we could find. Why would we want to give them
anything other then an even playing field?

> > Discourages PTW: Seating ceremony paints a big fat bullseye-target on
> > the top seed, thereby providing a DISINCENTIVE to play his best in the
> > last round of the tournament if he already has 2 GWs.
>
> I've heard this in this thread, but I don't think it holds water.
> #2 wants to beat #1 while achieving tie-or-better vs. #3-#5.
> #3 wants to beat #1-#2 while achieving tie-or-better vs #4-#5.
> #3 doesn't have any incentive to wreck #1 for #2 to win.

All I am saying is that it is not good to be regarded as the biggest
threat on the table. If #1 wins, everyone else loses.
